setup.zh: 你一个人了。娘在油灯底下一篇一篇地教你《吐纳经》：鼻子吸一口，闭住，心里数到一百二十，鼻子底下一根鹅毛，吐气的时候不许动。头一夜，你数到十二。
setup.en: You're on your own now. Under the oil lamp your mother teaches you *The Classic of Breathing* one section at a time: breathe in through the nose, hold it, count in your head to a hundred and twenty, a goose feather under your nose that mustn't stir when you breathe out. The first night, you reach twelve.

recap.zh: 一冬：娘在油灯下一篇一篇教你《吐纳经》，数从十二爬到五十二；马小宝穿上八两银子的狐皮袄，木牌烫了三下；刘豆芽告了密，爹替你坐上了柴垛；过了年，你十三了；开春，雁毛一换，又回到「毛飞」。
recap.en: A winter: your mother taught you *The Classic of Breathing* section by section by lamplight, and the count climbed from twelve to fifty-two; Ma Xiaobao put on an eight-tael fox-fur jacket and the token burned three times; Liu Douya told on you, and your father sat on the woodpile in your place; past the New Year, you were thirteen; in spring the wild-goose down put you back to "feather flew".

en: Top of the woodpile: one goose feather.
"Man: twelve. Feather flew, landed in henhouse."

story.zh:
九月十九，子时。石坳村最冷的地方，是沈家屋后那座柴垛的顶上。沈小满盘腿坐在那里，鼻子底下横着一片削薄的竹篾，竹篾上粘着一根鹅毛。

鹅毛是老周家那只大白鹅身上的，白天拔的。拔的时候，那鹅叫了半个村子，阿禾站在旁边，拿指头在脑门上点了一点：「鹅毛一根。鹅疼。利息另算。」

小满从鼻子里悄悄吸进一口气，吸满了，闭住，心里数：一，二，三……数要像他娘拨算盘珠子，一颗是一颗，不许赶。数到九，胸口发胀；数到十一，喉咙里像塞了一团棉絮；数到十二，那口气自己撞开了嘴，「噗」的一声，鹅毛从竹篾上飞了出去，在月光底下翻了三个跟头，落进了柴垛底下的鸡窝。鸡窝里一阵大乱。小满趴在柴垛边上，望着那黑洞洞的鸡窝，心想：书上说，要数到一百二十。吐气的时候，那根毛还得一动不动。

他爹说过，打猎最难的功夫不是拉弓，是蹲：蹲一头鹿，有时候要蹲三天三夜，鹿不来，不是鹿不在，是你蹲得还不够久。小满如今蹲的，是一根鹅毛。

第二天一早，他娘在灶前记账。她的账是一叠裁齐了的草纸，记的是米面油盐，一笔一笔，工工整整。这天早上，「盐二两，十六文」底下，多了一行：

九月十九。子时。满，十二。毛飞，落鸡窝。

这一天，离明年九月初九沉鼎观开山门，还有三百四十来天。这个日子，石坳村没有一个人知道，小满自己也不知道。他只知道，离一百二十，还差一百零八。

这根鹅毛的来历，要从前一夜那卷竹简说起。

洗髓以后，小满身上多了一把用不完的力气。挑水，两桶水在肩上轻得像两只空桶，他只好一步一挨，嘴里「嗨」一声，挑得满头大汗——那汗是憋出来的。劈柴，一斧子下去从头裂到底，一个早上劈出一座小山，他便把大半塞进柴垛最底下，拿旧柴盖了，只留一小堆在外头，坐在旁边假装喘气。他爹一瘸一拐地过来，看了看那一小堆，又看了看柴垛，道：「这柴垛，怎么高了一截？」小满道：「……风吹的。」他爹想了一想，觉得风大约是会把柴垛吹高的，便走了。那天晚上吃饭，他爹说这孩子今年长了力气，大约是吃了鹿肉的缘故。他娘在灶前头也不回：「哪块鹿肉？」那头鹿，皮、肉、角都给马三拿去了，一家三口，连一口鹿汤都没喝上。他爹张了张嘴，道：「……闻，闻也算。」

那卷竹简，是洗髓后第四天夜里拿出来的。他等他爹的呼噜打到第三遍——他爹的呼噜是分遍的，头一遍像拉锯，第二遍像推磨，第三遍像一头老牛过河，打到第三遍，天塌下来也醒不了——才把竹简捧到灶间。他娘就着那盏黄豆大的油灯，手指一个字一个字地摸过去，摸到第一行末尾，停住了。那一行是「吹呴呼吸，吐故纳新」。她道：「这一句……你外公念过。」

小满没见过外公。外公是镇上的穷塾师，死在他出生前头。他娘抬起头来：「这是……哪来的？」「山里捡的。」「……跟那条围脖一起捡的？」小满胸口那块木牌贴着心口，一动不动。他想起银月那句「你娘，用不着你说」，便道：「……嗯。」他娘便不再问了。

她从头念到尾，念得很慢，后头的字，有一半她也不认得。念完了，她把竹简卷上，道：「你外公要是在，他懂。」停了一停，又道：「他也未必懂。他念这些，是念着玩的。」小满急道：「那怎么练？」他娘是石坳村头一个会算账的人，碰上算不清的账，只有一个法子：「不知道值多少，就先数。」她把竹简又摊开，一直摊到倒数第二片，指着上头一行道：「通篇只有这一句有数。心里数到一百二十，拿一根鸿毛搁在鼻子底下，吐气的时候，毛不许动。」「鸿毛是什么毛？」「大雁的毛。」「大雁都飞南边去了。」他娘想了想：「先拿老周家的鹅凑合。开春雁回来了，再换。」

小满掰着指头算了算，道：「一百二十……娘，人又不是鱼。」他娘没忍住，「扑哧」一声笑了出来。

便在这时，里屋他爹的呼噜，断了。不是打完一遍换一遍的那种断，是半截里「咯」的一声，断得干干净净。娘儿俩一齐转过头去，望着那道门帘。过了好一会儿，那呼噜才又响起来，响得格外卖力，一口气从头一遍直接跳到了第三遍。

小满看着他娘。他娘看着那盏灯，把灯芯掐短了一点，道：「念下一句。」

他爹醒着。醒着，却装睡。他爹这辈子，没撒过一句谎。

头一课，是竹简最前头的两句。他娘说，那两句是开篇，先认头，再认身子。

「吐故纳新，」他娘道，「就是把旧的吐出去，把新的吸进来。」她顿了一顿，眼睛看着那盏灯，又道：「人，也一样。」小满问人怎么一样，她没有答，只念下一句：「真人之息以踵，众人之息以喉。」她拿手指在桌上比划，「真人喘一口气，一直喘到脚后跟；众人喘气，喘到嗓子眼就完了。」

小满想了一想，道：「那我是众人。」他娘道：「你是众人。」

那天夜里，小满头一个想法是：既然要喘到脚后跟，脚后跟总得先知道有这回事。他脱了鞋，光着脚站在下了霜的院子里，一口一口往下吸，吸了小半个时辰，脚后跟没觉出什么气来，倒先冻木了。第二天，他走路一瘸一拐。他爹瞧见了，道：「你也瘸了？」小满道：「学你。」他娘在灶前道：「书上说的是息，不是脚。」

第二夜，他老老实实坐回柴垛上，一口一口地试。他这才觉出来，自己吸气，是拿嗓子「吞」的，一口吞进来，堵在胸口，胸口一胀，数就断。他便试着让那口气往下走，走过胸口，走到肚子，再往下——脚后跟是走不到的，走到肚子就不肯走了。可这一往下，胸口便松了一松，数到十二，还能再挤三下。

九月廿四。满，十九。毛飞，落柴堆。

每夜数完了，他都要把木牌掏出来，捧在手心里，跟它报一报这一天的账：「今儿，挑水四担，装累两回。劈柴一担，藏柴半担。数到十九，毛飞了。」木牌不答。报完了塞回衣领里，那木牌总是温的，他便以为，是自己拿手捂热的。白天，还有不吐纳的夜里，它是凉的。

他娘记完这一笔，把竹简翻到第二篇，道：「这一篇，说是最老的一篇。刻在玉上的。」小满凑过去看，那一篇上「深」「蓄」「伸」「下」……十个字一个压一个，像一架梯子。他心里一动：一架梯子，一夜爬完它。

十月初二，他娘念第二篇。那一篇没有整句，只有十个字，一级一级排下去：深、蓄、伸、下、定、固、萌、长、退、天。末了一行小字，说走顺了是活路，走乱了要命。

她拿指头一个字一个字地点：吸得深，才存得住；存满了往下走，沉到底，定住；定牢了，像种子一样发芽、长大；长满了，顺着原路退回来，一直退到头顶——「退则天。」小满眼睛亮了：「到天上？」他娘道：「书上是这么写的。」

十个台阶，一口气。小满那天夜里上了柴垛，盘腿一坐，吸一大口，心里一步一步地往上赶：深，蓄，伸，下——那口气在肚子里转了半圈，他哪里等得及它自己「定」，一使劲，硬往下压；压到「萌」，胸口里「咯」的一声，像一口井给人拿石头堵了，那口气上不来，下不去，在嗓子眼里一翻，他便咳了起来。

这一咳，就停不住了。他趴在柴垛上，咳得眼泪鼻涕一齐往下流，咳得鸡窝里的鸡也醒了。里屋的呼噜断了。门「吱呀」一响，一盏灯晃了出来，他爹拖着那条腿，一步一步走到柴垛底下，把灯举高了：「谁在上头？」

小满一把将鹅毛塞进了嘴里，屁股底下压住那卷竹简，憋着咳，道：「……爹，我、我出来看雪。」他爹道：「雪还没下。」「……等它下。」他爹举着灯，看了他很久，看得小满嘴里那根鹅毛都湿透了。然后他的眼睛往下一落，落在儿子屁股底下那一截露出来的竹片上，停了一停。他道：「上头风大。」便拖着腿回去了。

小满把鹅毛从嘴里吐出来，在柴垛上坐到后半夜，也没想明白，他爹那一眼，看见了没有。

第二天夜里，他数到十一，便憋不住了。第三天，还是十一。

十月初三。满，十一。毛飞。
十月初四。十一。

他娘看着这两行，没说他，只说了两个字：「别急。」她道：「你外公教我打算盘，头一句，也是这两个字。」「打算盘也会死人？」「算错了，一家子饿死。」

她教他打算盘，他哪里坐得住，拨了三下，心又飞到柴垛上去了。他娘教烦了，从灶台上抓过一把栗子——那是秋天他在后山捡的，统共没几颗，留着过年的——在桌上摆了九个，三排，每排三个，拿指甲在栗子上一颗一颗刻道道，头顶那颗刻九道，脚底下那颗刻一道。她道：「你外公教我算账，头一样教的，不是加减，是这个。」她一面挪，一面念：「戴九履一，左三右七，二四为肩，六八为足，五居中央。」

小满横着加：四、九、二，十五；三、五、七，十五；八、一、六，十五。竖着加，十五。斜着加，还是十五。他加得眼睛都直了：「娘，这栗子成精了。」他娘道：「不是栗子成精。是这九个数，本来就这么待着，各在各的格子里，谁也不抢谁的。你外公说，这叫洛书，古书上只说是洛水里出来的，驮它的老龟，是后人添的。」她又道：「你外公说，这是他从一本旧书上看来的。那本书，后来不知道哪里去了。」

小满不管老龟，他只盯着那九颗栗子，忽然明白了那块玉上的十个字：深是深，蓄是蓄，一个字一个格子，谁也不许抢谁的。他那一夜，是让「萌」去抢了「定」的格子。走顺了是活路，走乱了要命。

从那以后，他一夜只走一格。一个格子走稳了，才走下一格。

十月初九。满，二十三。毛翻了个身，没飞。

他掰着指头算：二十天，涨了十一，照这么一格一格走下去，一百二十，明年五月准到。他觉得这日子还早，不着急。

冬月十四，老周家添了个小子，是阿禾的弟弟。第二天夜里，他娘念第三篇：「载营魄袌一，能无离乎？专气致柔，能如婴儿乎？」那个「袌」字，她说古人写的就是「抱」。前一句她也讲不大清，只说是身子和魂儿抱在一起，不分家；后一句小满抢着讲：「专气致揉，就是把气揉一揉，揉软了。」他娘拿指头在那个字上敲了一敲：「柔。气要柔，柔得像刚生下来的孩子。」

「刚生下来的孩子，怎么喘气？」「你去看。」

小满便以还鹅毛利息为名，钻进了老周家。那孩子睡在炕头，裹在一床小被子里，红通通的，皱巴巴的，像一只剥了皮的小老鼠。阿禾守在炕沿上，手里缝着她那件旧袄的衬里，一针一针，缝进去的是一粒一粒的谷子。她见他进来，道：「看可以。看一回，半个鸡蛋。」小满道：「记账。」又问她缝的什么。阿禾道：「禾种。今年坡田少收了两成，我挑了三十粒最饱的。」她拿下巴点了点炕头的弟弟，「多了一张嘴。地再不长，他吃什么？」说完便不理他了。小满便趴在炕沿上看。

他看了半个时辰，看出一件怪事：那孩子喘气，胸口一动不动，动的是肚子。肚子一鼓，一瘪，一鼓，一瘪，慢得像在数数，一点声音也没有。他把手搁在自己肚子上，吸一口气——鼓起来的是胸口。原来他长到十二岁，连喘气都长歪了。阿禾在旁边拿炭条记道：「看娃，半个时辰。利息另算。」

那天夜里，他照着那孩子的样子，把气吸进肚子里，肚子一鼓，胸口不动。数到二十，胸口还是松的。

冬月十六。满，三十一。毛翻。

同一页竹简上还有一句：「致虚极，守静笃。」他娘说，这是教人心里要空，空到底；要静，静到底。小满觉得这一句最容易：柴垛上半夜三更，要多静有多静。他想错了。

冬月廿二，马三来收山风钱。这山风钱，是有一年小满他爹喝了二两酒，小声问了一句「那山上的风，也姓马吗」，第二天马家就开始收的，一个人头五十文。马三拿短棍一下一下敲着门框，他爹捧出一百五十文，那是他娘从过年的饺子钱里挪出来的。马小宝跟在后头，身上穿着一件新的狐皮袄子，火红火红，毛领子一直围到下巴，把他那张圆脸托在当中，活像一盘端上桌的红烧狮子头。

他走到小满跟前，眼睛一转，落在他领口露出的一截红绳上：「脖子上挂的什么？」手已经伸了过来，一把扯出了那块木牌。小满浑身的血一下子凉了。马小宝把木牌翻过来掉过去看了两眼，一块巴掌大的旧木头，刻着一只蜷着的狐狸，灰扑扑的。日头底下，那条尾巴一点光也不见，木头凉得像块冰。他撇撇嘴：「破木头。」往雪地里一扔。小满扑过去捡起来，拍掉了雪，攥在手心里，低着头道：「吴婆婆给的护身符。」马小宝没再理它，拿那只捏着桂花糕的手，摸着领子上那圈狐狸毛：「沈小满，看见没？真狐狸。八两银子。你家一年的租才二两，我这一件袄子，顶你家四年。」他把领子竖起来，又放下去，「狐狸就是好，暖和。你摸摸？」小满低着头道：「不摸了，小宝哥。我手脏。」马小宝很满意，嚼着桂花糕走了。小满一抬眼，看见他娘站在门里头，两只手拢在袖子里。她那件棉袄的袖子短了一截，一拢，手腕便露在外头，冻得发红。

那天夜里，他坐在柴垛上，吸一口气，眼前是那一团火红；再吸一口，是他娘的手腕。他把念头往下压，压下去一个，浮上来两个。数到五，那口气就散了。正在这时，胸口那块木牌，烫了一下。

这一下烫得极狠，像有人拿烧红的火筷子在他心口上戳了一戳。他「嗷」的一声，险些从柴垛上翻下去。他把木牌掏出来，捧在手心里，小声道：「……你也看见了？」木牌又烫了一下。自打她化光钻进去，这木牌只会一明一暗地喘气，他报了几十夜的账，它一回也没答过。他道：「那件袄子？」

木牌第三次烫了一下，烫得他手心通红，只好把它扔在棉絮上。他对着手心吹气，心里先想起了镇上说书先生讲的孙猴子：祖师在他头上敲了三下，是叫他三更天从后门进去，传他本事。木牌烫三下，莫非也是暗号？他想了半天，想不出该从哪个后门进去，吹着吹着，倒明白过来了：那一圈火红的毛，是狐狸毛。她是一只狐狸。他把木牌捡起来，小声道：「好好好，记账，记账。我记着呢。」木牌这才慢慢凉下去，一明，一暗，又回到那个样子，像一个人在很深很深的地方睡觉。

冬月廿二。满，七。毛飞。牌烫三下。

七。比九月十九那一夜还少五个。

第二天夜里，他娘没有念竹简，给他讲了一个故事。她说，这故事是外公讲给她听的：有一个读书人，带着学生路过一片林子，看见一个驼背的老头，拿一根竹竿粘知了，一粘一个，跟在地上捡的一样。读书人问他有什么诀窍。老头说，五六月里，我在竿头上摞泥丸，摞两个不掉，摞三个不掉，摞到五个不掉，粘知了便像捡了；我站着，像一截树桩子；我举着胳膊，像一根枯树枝；天底下那么大，东西那么多，我眼里只有一只知了的翅膀。读书人回头对学生说：「用志不分，乃凝于神。」那读书人便是孔子，你外公说，这是庄子书上的。

他娘讲完了，问道：「马小宝那件袄子，是知了的翅膀么？」小满道：「不是。」「那就别看。」第三天夜里，他爬上柴垛前，他娘问：「那件袄子，什么颜色？」「……红的。」「再去坐。」第四天夜里，她又问：「什么颜色？」小满想了一想：「忘了。」他娘道：「好。」

冬月廿四。满，三十四。毛翻。

他不看了。可他不知道，那几天夜里，柴垛底下有一双眼睛，在看他。

The nineteenth of the ninth month, the hour of Zi. The coldest place in Shi'ao Village was the top of the woodpile behind the Shens' house. Shen Xiaoman sat there cross-legged, a thin-shaved strip of bamboo held under his nose, and a goose feather stuck to the bamboo.

The feather came off Old Zhou's big white goose, plucked that afternoon. The goose had honked half the village awake, and A He, standing by, tapped her forehead with one finger: "One goose feather. Goose hurt. Interest charged separately."

Xiaoman drew a breath in quietly through his nose, drew it full, held it, and counted in his head: one, two, three… The counting had to be like his mother flicking abacus beads, one bead at a time, no hurrying. At nine his chest swelled; at eleven his throat felt stuffed with cotton wool; at twelve the breath burst his mouth open by itself — *pff* — and the feather flew off the bamboo, turned three somersaults in the moonlight and landed in the henhouse at the foot of the woodpile. The henhouse erupted. Xiaoman lay flat on the edge of the woodpile, staring down at that black hole of a henhouse, thinking: the book says count to a hundred and twenty. And while you breathe out, the feather mustn't move at all.

His father used to say the hardest skill in hunting isn't drawing the bow, it's the waiting crouch: you crouch for a deer three days and three nights sometimes, and if the deer doesn't come, it isn't that the deer isn't there — it's that you haven't crouched long enough. What Xiaoman was crouching for now was a feather.

Early next morning his mother kept her accounts by the stove. Her ledger was a stack of trimmed straw paper for rice, flour, oil and salt, entry by entry, neat and square. That morning, under "Salt, two ounces, sixteen cash", there was one line more:

Ninth month, nineteenth. Hour of Zi. Man: twelve. Feather flew, landed in henhouse.

That day there were some three hundred and forty days left until the ninth of the ninth month next year, when Chending Temple would open its gate. Not one person in Shi'ao Village knew that date, Xiaoman included. All he knew was that he was a hundred and eight short of a hundred and twenty.

Where that feather came from begins with the bamboo scroll, the night before.

Since the marrow-washing, Xiaoman had strength he couldn't use up. Carrying water, the two full buckets on his shoulder weighed like two empty ones, so he had to shuffle along going "hup!" and arrive drenched in sweat — sweat squeezed out on purpose. Chopping wood, one swing split a log top to bottom and a morning made a small mountain, so he stuffed most of it into the bottom of the woodpile, covered it with old wood, left a little heap outside and sat by it pretending to pant. His father limped over, looked at the little heap, looked at the woodpile. "How's the pile got a layer taller?" Xiaoman said, "…The wind blew it." His father thought about it, decided the wind probably could blow a woodpile taller, and went away. At supper his father said the boy had got strong this year, likely from eating the venison. His mother, at the stove, didn't turn round. "Which venison?" The hide, the meat and the antlers had all gone to Ma San; the three of them hadn't had so much as a mouthful of venison broth. His father opened his mouth. "…Smelling it, smelling it counts."

The bamboo scroll came out on the fourth night after the marrow-washing. He waited till his father's snoring reached its third round — his father snored in rounds: the first like a saw, the second like a millstone, the third like an old ox crossing a river, and by the third the sky could fall without waking him — and only then carried the scroll to the kitchen. By the bean-sized flame of the oil lamp his mother ran a finger over it character by character, and at the end of the first line she stopped. The line was *Blow, puff, exhale, inhale; spit out the old, take in the new.* She said, "This line… your grandfather used to recite it."

Xiaoman had never seen his grandfather — a poor village schoolmaster who had died before he was born. His mother looked up. "Where… did this come from?" "Found it in the mountains." "…Found it along with that scarf of yours?" The token lay still against Xiaoman's heart. He remembered the fox's words — *Your mother doesn't need you to tell her* — and said, "…Mm." His mother asked nothing more.

She read it from start to end, very slowly; half the later characters she didn't know either. When she'd finished she rolled it up and said, "If your grandfather were here, he'd understand it." She paused. "Or maybe not. He recited these things for fun." Xiaoman said anxiously, "Then how do I practise?" His mother was the best reckoner in Shi'ao Village, and for an account she couldn't reckon she had only one method: "When you don't know what it's worth, count first." She unrolled the scroll again, all the way to the second-to-last slip, and pointed to a line. "This is the only line in the whole thing with a number in it. Count in your head to a hundred and twenty, put a wild-goose feather under your nose, and when you breathe out, the feather mustn't move." "What's a wild-goose feather?" "A feather off a wild goose." "The wild geese have all flown south." His mother thought. "Make do with Old Zhou's goose for now. When the wild geese come back in spring, change it."

Xiaoman counted on his fingers. "A hundred and twenty… Mum, people aren't fish." His mother couldn't help it; she snorted out a laugh.

Just then, in the inner room, his father's snoring broke off. Not the break between one round and the next — it stopped halfway with a *hk*, clean as a cut rope. Mother and son turned together to look at the door curtain. After a good while the snoring started again, very hard-working, jumping straight from the first round to the third.

Xiaoman looked at his mother. His mother looked at the lamp, pinched the wick a little shorter, and said, "Read the next line."

His father was awake. Awake, and pretending to sleep. His father had never told a lie in his life.

The first lesson was the first two lines of the scroll. His mother said those two were the opening: learn the head first, then the body.

"Spit out the old, take in the new," his mother said. "It means breathe out what's old and breathe in what's new." She paused, eyes on the lamp. "People, too." Xiaoman asked how people too; she didn't answer, only read the next line: "*The true man breathes from his heels; the common man breathes from his throat.*" She sketched it on the table with a finger. "A true man's breath goes all the way down to his heels; ordinary people's breath stops at the throat."

Xiaoman thought. "Then I'm the common man." His mother said, "You're the common man."

That night Xiaoman's first idea was: if the breath is to go to the heels, the heels ought to know about it first. He took off his shoes and stood barefoot in the frosted yard, drawing breath down, mouthful after mouthful, for the best part of half an hour; his heels felt no breath at all, only went numb with cold. Next day he walked with a limp. His father saw. "You lame too?" Xiaoman said, "Copying you." His mother said from the stove, "The book says breath, not feet."

The second night he sat back on the woodpile like a good boy and tried it mouthful by mouthful. Only then did he notice that he drew breath by *swallowing* it with his throat — a gulp, stuck in his chest, the chest swelled, and the count broke. So he tried letting the breath go down, past the chest to the belly, and further — it wouldn't go as far as the heels; at the belly it refused to go on. But going down that far, his chest loosened a little, and after twelve he could squeeze out three more.

Ninth month, twenty-fourth. Man: nineteen. Feather flew, landed in woodpile.

Every night when he'd finished counting he took out the token, held it in his palm, and reported the day's accounts to it: "Today, four loads of water, pretended to be tired twice. One load of firewood chopped, half a load hidden. Counted to nineteen; the feather flew." The token didn't answer. When he'd done and tucked it back inside his collar, the token was always warm, and he supposed it was his own hand that had warmed it. By day, and on nights he didn't practise, it was cool.

When his mother had entered it, she turned the scroll to the second section. "This one, it says, is the oldest. Carved on jade." Xiaoman leaned in to look: *deep*, *store*, *stretch*, *down*… ten characters stacked one on another, like a ladder. His heart jumped: a ladder — climb the whole thing in one night.

On the second of the tenth month his mother read the second section. It had no sentences at all, only ten characters going down rung by rung: *deep, store, stretch, down, settle, firm, sprout, grow, return, heaven.* At the end, one line of small script: keep to the order and it is the road to life; muddle it and it will kill you.

She pointed with a finger, character by character: breathe deep and it can be stored; stored full, it goes down, sinks to the bottom and settles; settled firm, it sprouts like a seed and grows; grown full, it comes back along the way it went, all the way up to the top of the head — "*returned, then heaven.*" Xiaoman's eyes lit up. "Up to heaven?" His mother said, "That's what the book says."

Ten rungs, one breath. That night Xiaoman climbed the woodpile, sat down cross-legged, took a big breath and hurried up the rungs in his head: deep, store, stretch, down — the breath turned half a circle in his belly, and he couldn't wait for it to *settle* on its own; he shoved it down hard; by *sprout* there was a *hk* in his chest, like a well stopped up with a rock; the breath couldn't go up or down, it flipped over in his throat, and he began to cough.

Once he started coughing he couldn't stop. He lay on the woodpile coughing till tears and snot ran together, coughing till the hens woke up. In the inner room the snoring broke off. The door creaked; a lamp swayed out; his father dragged his leg step by step to the foot of the woodpile and held the lamp up high. "Who's up there?"

Xiaoman stuffed the goose feather into his mouth, sat on the bamboo scroll, and, choking back the cough, said, "…Dad, I, I came out to look at the snow." His father said, "It hasn't snowed yet." "…Waiting for it to." His father held up the lamp and looked at him a long time — so long the feather in Xiaoman's mouth was soaked through. Then his eyes dropped to the end of a bamboo slip sticking out from under his son's backside, and rested there a moment. He said, "Windy up there," and dragged his leg back inside.

Xiaoman spat the feather out and sat on the woodpile till the small hours, and still couldn't make out whether his father had seen or not.

The next night he could hold only to eleven. The night after, eleven again.

Tenth month, third. Man: eleven. Feather flew.
Tenth month, fourth. Eleven.

His mother looked at those two lines and didn't scold him; she said just two words: "Don't hurry." She said, "When your grandfather taught me the abacus, those were the first two words too." "The abacus can kill you?" "Reckon wrong, and a whole family starves."

She set about teaching him the abacus, but he couldn't sit still; three flicks and his mind had flown back to the woodpile. His mother lost patience, grabbed a handful of chestnuts from the stove — the ones he'd picked up on the back hill in autumn, not many of them, saved for New Year — and set out nine on the table in three rows of three, scratching lines on each with her nail: nine on the one at the top, one on the one at the bottom. She said, "When your grandfather taught me reckoning, the first thing he taught wasn't adding and taking away. It was this." Moving them as she spoke, she chanted: "*Wear nine, tread one; three on the left, seven on the right; two and four the shoulders, six and eight the feet; five in the middle.*"

Xiaoman added across: four, nine, two, fifteen; three, five, seven, fifteen; eight, one, six, fifteen. Down: fifteen. Corner to corner: fifteen again. He added till his eyes went glassy. "Mum, these chestnuts have turned into spirits." His mother said, "It's not that the chestnuts are spirits. These nine numbers just sit like this — each in its own square, none grabbing another's. Your grandfather said it's called the Luo Writing. The old books only say it came out of the Luo River; the turtle carrying it was added later." She added, "Your grandfather said he got it from an old book. What became of that book, nobody knows."

Xiaoman didn't care about the turtle; he stared at the nine chestnuts and suddenly understood those ten characters on the jade: deep is deep, store is store, one character to a square, none allowed to grab another's. That night he'd let *sprout* grab *settle*'s square. Keep to the order and it's the road to life; muddle it and it'll kill you.

From then on he went one square a night. Only when one square was steady did he go on to the next.

Tenth month, ninth. Man: twenty-three. Feather turned over, didn't fly.

He counted on his fingers: twenty days, up eleven; go on square by square like this and a hundred and twenty would be there by fifth month next year for sure. He thought that was still a long way off. No hurry.

On the fourteenth of the eleventh month Old Zhou's family had a boy — A He's little brother. The next night his mother read the third section: "*Holding body and soul embraced as one — can you keep them from parting? Gathering the breath to utmost softness — can you be like a newborn babe?*" The odd character for *embrace*, she said, was just how the ancients wrote it. The first line she couldn't really explain either — only that body and soul hold each other and don't come apart. The second, Xiaoman jumped in to explain: "Gathering the breath to utmost *knead*-ness — you knead the breath a bit and knead it soft." His mother tapped that character with a finger. "*Soft.* The breath must be soft, soft as a baby just born."

"How does a baby just born breathe?" "Go and look."

So Xiaoman, on the pretext of paying interest on the goose feather, slipped into Old Zhou's house. The baby lay at the head of the kang wrapped in a little quilt, red and wrinkled, like a skinned baby mouse. A He was keeping guard at the edge of the kang, sewing the lining of her old padded jacket, stitch by stitch — and what she was sewing in was grains of rice, one at a time. When he came in she said, "You can look. Half an egg a look." Xiaoman said, "Put it on account," and asked what she was sewing. A He said, "Seed grain. The slope field brought in two-tenths less this year. I picked the thirty fullest grains." She jerked her chin at her little brother at the head of the kang. "One more mouth. If the land won't grow, what's he going to eat?" And she paid him no more mind. So Xiaoman leaned over the kang to look.

He looked for half an hour and noticed something odd: when the baby breathed, its chest didn't move at all; what moved was its belly. The belly rose, fell, rose, fell, slow as counting, without a sound. He put a hand on his own belly and breathed in — what rose was his chest. So he'd grown to twelve and even his breathing had grown crooked. A He, beside him, wrote with her charcoal: "Looked at baby, half an hour. Interest charged separately."

That night he breathed the way the baby did, into the belly: the belly rose, the chest stayed still. At twenty his chest was still loose.

Eleventh month, sixteenth. Man: thirty-one. Feather turned over.

On the same slip there was another line: "*Attain emptiness to the utmost; keep stillness steadfast.*" His mother said it taught you to make the mind empty, empty to the bottom; still, still to the bottom. Xiaoman thought that line the easiest of all: on a woodpile in the dead of night, there was all the stillness you could want. He was wrong.

On the twenty-second of the eleventh month Ma San came to collect the mountain-wind money. The mountain-wind money dated from the year Xiaoman's father had two ounces of wine and asked, very quietly, "Is the wind on the mountain named Ma too?" — the next day the Mas started collecting it, fifty cash a head. Ma San rapped the doorframe with his club, over and over; his father brought out a hundred and fifty cash, which his mother had moved over from the New Year dumpling money. Ma Xiaobao followed behind in a new fox-fur jacket, fiery red, the fur collar right up to his chin, holding his round face in the middle like a plate of red-braised lion's-head meatball brought to the table.

He came up to Xiaoman and his eyes slid to a bit of red cord showing at his collar. "What's that round your neck?" His hand was already out; he yanked the token free. The blood in Xiaoman's whole body went cold. Ma Xiaobao turned it over twice: an old bit of wood the size of a palm, carved with a curled-up fox, grey and dull. In the daylight the tail showed no light at all, and the wood was cold as ice. He curled his lip. "Junk wood," and tossed it in the snow. Xiaoman dived for it, brushed off the snow, clutched it in his fist, and said with his head down, "A charm Granny Wu gave me." Ma Xiaobao paid it no more mind; with the hand that held his osmanthus cake he stroked the ring of fox fur at his collar. "See this, Shen Xiaoman? Real fox. Eight taels of silver. Your family's rent for a year is only two; this one jacket is four years of your family." He turned the collar up, then down again. "Fox is great. Warm. Want to feel?" Xiaoman, head down, said, "Better not, Brother Xiaobao. My hands are dirty." Ma Xiaobao was very pleased and went off chewing his cake. Xiaoman looked up and saw his mother standing inside the door, hands tucked in her sleeves. The sleeves of her coat were too short; tucked in, her wrists showed outside, red with cold.

That night he sat on the woodpile: one breath, and there was that ball of fiery red before his eyes; another, and it was his mother's wrists. He pushed the thoughts down; push one down, two floated up. At five the breath fell apart. Just then the token on his chest burned, once.

It burned viciously, as if someone had jabbed his heart with a red-hot poker. He yelped and nearly toppled off the woodpile. He took out the token and held it in his palm and whispered, "…You saw it too?" The token burned again. Since she'd turned to light and slipped inside, all the token had ever done was breathe, bright and dim; he'd reported the day's accounts to it for dozens of nights and it had never once answered. He said, "The jacket?"

The token burned a third time, so hot his palm went red and he had to drop it on the cotton quilt. Blowing on his palm, he first thought of the Monkey King the storyteller in town told about: the master rapped him on the head three times, meaning come by the back door at the third watch, and I'll teach you. Three burns from the token — was that a secret signal too? He thought hard and couldn't work out which back door to go in by; and as he blew, he understood instead: that ring of fiery-red fur was fox fur. She was a fox. He picked up the token and whispered, "All right, all right, it's on account, on account. I've got it written down." Only then did the token slowly cool, bright, dim, back to how it was, like someone sleeping somewhere very, very deep.

Eleventh month, twenty-second. Man: seven. Feather flew. Token burned three times.

Seven. Five fewer than that first night of the ninth month.

The next night his mother didn't read the scroll; she told him a story instead, one his grandfather had told her. A scholar was passing through a wood with his students and saw a hunchbacked old man catching cicadas with a bamboo pole, one per try, as easy as picking them off the ground. The scholar asked his secret. The old man said: in the fifth and sixth months I stack clay pellets on the tip of the pole — two without falling, three without falling, and when five don't fall, catching cicadas is like picking them up. I stand like a tree stump; I hold my arm like a dry branch; heaven and earth are vast and things are many, but all I know is one cicada's wing. The scholar turned to his students: "*When the will is undivided, it gathers into spirit.*" The scholar was Confucius; your grandfather said it's in the book of Zhuangzi.

When she'd finished, his mother asked, "Is Ma Xiaobao's jacket a cicada's wing?" Xiaoman said, "No." "Then don't look at it." The third night, before he climbed the woodpile, his mother asked: "That jacket — what colour?" "…Red." "Go and sit again." The fourth night she asked again: "What colour?" Xiaoman thought. "Forgot." His mother said, "Good."

Eleventh month, twenty-fourth. Man: thirty-four. Feather turned over.

He stopped looking. But he didn't know that for several nights now, from the foot of the woodpile, a pair of eyes had been looking at him.

story.zh:
那双眼睛是刘豆芽的。刘豆芽是老刘家的大小子，比小满小半岁，瘦得像一根豆芽，冬天夜里下网捉麻雀，一只卖两文。腊月初十那天夜里，他蹲在沈家柴垛底下收网，一抬头，看见柴垛顶上冒白气——冒一口，停老半天，再冒一口。三九天里，人喘气是要冒白气的；那白气停得太久了，久得不像活人。头一夜，他看见那人憋完了气，从脖子上掏出一块木头，捧在手心里嘀嘀咕咕，像在跟它报账；第二夜也是。第三夜，他爬近了看，柴垛顶上坐着一个人，鼻子底下横着一根毛。

「沈小满，你拿鹅毛干啥？」小满差点从柴垛上栽下来。刘豆芽已经爬上来了，眼睛骨碌碌地转：「你夜夜在这儿。我看了三夜了。憋完了气，还跟一块木头说话——你在念咒？你不说，我明儿告诉马小宝。」

小满脑子飞快地转了三圈。说实话，是死；说不知道，他明儿照样去告。他道：「比憋气。谁憋得久，谁赢。我跟鹅毛比，它不动，我不许喘。」刘豆芽眼睛一亮：「我也比！」

他抓过鹅毛，往鼻子底下一搁，腮帮子一鼓，吸得像一只风箱，脑袋一点一个数，点得跟鸡啄米似的，比小满快了一倍，脸由红变紫，由紫变黑，点到第四十四下，那口气「砰」地炸了出来。鹅毛像给火铳打中的麻雀，直飞过院子，落进了猪圈。刘豆芽扶着柴垛喘了半天，喘匀了，大叫：「四十四！你呢？」小满道：「……三十七。」

刘豆芽乐得在柴垛上打滚：「你夜夜练，还不如我头一回！明儿我告诉全村！」小满道：「说吧。」这话倒是真心的：全村人知道沈小满憋气输给了刘豆芽，比知道他在练仙人的东西，强一百倍。

可他爬进猪圈捡鹅毛的时候，心里还是凉了半截。他夜夜数，数了快三个月，数不过一个头一回来的刘豆芽。

腊月里，他给吴婆婆送了一担柴。那柴，就是他藏在柴垛最底下的那一半，再藏下去，柴垛就要塌了。

吴婆婆坐在门槛上，听他一根一根码柴，听完了，道：「一担。一个人挑的。挑得不喘。」小满这才想起来要喘，忙喘了两口。吴婆婆那三颗牙便露了出来：「现在喘，晚了。」她又说她那三颗牙，还在，还没等到。小满问等什么，她说：「等到了，它就知道了。」她伸手摸了摸他的手，凑到鼻子底下闻了闻：「后院的土？」小满道：「我爹翻的。说土酸了，一股锈味儿。」吴婆婆朝着西边，好一会儿，才道：「那时候，这地，是香的。」

从吴婆婆家回来，路过打谷场，孩子们在玩九头蛇。一个大些的孩子当蛇头，后头的一个揪着一个的后衣襟，揪成一串，每人一只手举在头顶，打头的「嘶」一声，后头的一个跟一个学，九张嘴一齐嘶嘶地响，好叫那捉蛇的分不清哪一个才是真的蛇头。会捉的不看，只听：头一声是热的，后头的，都是回声。当蛇头的，正是刘豆芽。一串人一面跑，一面唱那首谁也不知道是谁编的老歌：

「一个头，吃一山，
两个头，吃两川，
三个头，吃三仓米，
四个头，吃四口田，
五个头，吃五谷种，
六个头，吃六畜圈，
七个头，吃七家灶，
八个头，吃八方烟，
九个头，吃九州——
吃完九州，还喊饿！」

唱到「七个头，吃七家灶」，歌声停了。马小宝穿着那件火红的狐皮袄子，嚼着桂花糕走了过来：「九头蛇？我也玩。我当蛇头。」刘豆芽慢慢放下胳膊，让开了。马小宝站过去，两只胳膊一张，「嘶」了一声。后头一个也没跟着学。那一串孩子，不知什么时候，已经散了，一个一个溜回自家门口，躲在娘身后探着脑袋看。马小宝一个人张着胳膊站在打谷场上，站了一会儿，骂了一句「没意思」，一脚踢飞了一块冻雪。门后头，不知哪个孩子小声唱了一句：「……吃完九州，还喊饿。」

老槐树底下，阿禾拿指头在脑门上一下一下地点：「一个头，一山；两个头，两川……」小满问她数这个做什么，她道：「九个头，吃了这么多东西。这账，得有人记着。」

小满正要笑，笑容僵在了脸上。打谷场那头，刘豆芽没走。马小宝从袖子里摸出一块桂花糕，递给了他。刘豆芽接过去，咬了一口，凑到马小宝耳朵边上，说了几句什么，一面说，一面拿手比了个巴掌大小，又朝沈家柴垛的方向，指了一指。

过年那天，沈家没有肉。他娘包了两盖帘白菜饺子，把馅儿往里多塞一点，塞得个个鼓着肚子，像是吃饱了的样子。天擦黑，阿禾端着一只碗过来了，满满一碗卤下水，酱色的，油汪汪的，往灶台上一搁：「我娘卤的。不是送的。秋天那一挂下水，比一颗白菜金贵，多出来的那一笔，我家欠你家的。这一碗，还本。利息，明年再说。」走到门口，又回头冲小满道：「你欠我的，还是三个半。过年不讨债。」

守岁的时候，他娘点了灯，念竹简第四篇：「恬惔虚无，真气从之，精神内守，病安从来。」他娘说：心里不贪，不急，空空的，那口「真气」才肯跟着你走。

小满只听进去一半。他心里揣着一个数：前一夜，他数到了四十六。今夜要是能过五十，新年就是个好兆头。他爬上柴垛——大年夜里，他娘由着他——喊一声「起」，吸一口气，闭住，心里数得飞快：三十，四十，四十五……他娘在窗户里头拨着算盘，一颗珠子，一个数。他那口气炸出来，大声道：「五十！」窗户里，他娘道：「三十八。」

小满愣在柴垛上。他娘把算盘推到窗台上：「我照你外公教的快慢，一颗一颗拨的。你数到五十，我拨到三十八。」她顿了一顿，「你这是替刘豆芽数的。天下的数，唯慢不破。」

小满脸上一阵发烧。他娘又道：「你知道你为什么叫小满？」「……小满那天生的。」「你爹要叫你满仓，说满仓满囤，一辈子吃得饱。我说不行。满了，就要溢出来。仓满了，老鼠就来了；碗满了，就洒了；人满了，就不知道自己吃饱了。小满，正好——饱了一点，还没满，还知道饿。」她把一颗剥好的栗子塞进他嘴里，「数也一样。你一贪，它就满了，满了，就洒了。」

除夕。报五十。实三十八。

过了子时，小满十三了。他把木牌掏出来，小声道：「过年好。我十三了。」木牌一明，一暗，还在睡。他把它贴回胸口，没再贪那个数，一呼一吸，一颗珠子一颗珠子地数，数到四十一，毛翻了个身，没飞。

村子里有人放了一个炮仗，远远地「砰」了一声。小满没去看，他在看打谷场的方向。打谷场上什么也没有，可他记着刘豆芽那一指。马小宝知道了。马小宝知道了，就不会只知道一半。

正月初四一早，他爹蹲在屋后的雪地里，看了半天。雪上一串小草鞋印子，从院墙外头绕进来，到柴垛底下便停，来过不止一回；昨夜又多了七八双靴子印，跟着那串小草鞋，绕着院墙走了一圈，在屋后站过，踩乱了一片。他爹站起来，拍了拍膝盖上的雪，只说了两个字：「踩点。」回屋躺下，呼噜打到了第三遍。

正月初五夜里，小满没上柴垛。

他躺在炕上，睁着眼睛，算了一整天的账：马小宝那种人，听见「柴垛上憋气」，想的不会是憋气，是「沈小满在藏东西」；想到这一层，他就要来翻。翻出一根鹅毛不要紧，翻出那卷竹简，翻出他胸口这块木牌——他把竹简塞进了炕洞，把木牌攥在手心里，听着外头。里屋他爹的呼噜，一遍一遍地打着。

子时前后，院墙外头亮起了火把。七八个，一晃一晃，是马家的家丁，打头的是那件火红的狐皮袄子。他们没进院门，从墙根绕到屋后，直奔柴垛。小满趴在窗缝上，一颗心跳到了嗓子眼：他爹的呼噜，不知什么时候停了。

火把围住了柴垛。柴垛顶上，坐着一个人，裹着那床破棉絮，一条腿直直地伸着，膝盖上缠着麻布，端端正正。是他爹。

马小宝举着火把，愣了半天：「……老瘸子？你在上头干什么？」他爹道：「膝盖疼，睡不着，出来问问天。」「问什么天？」「明儿要下雪。」马小宝往四下里照了照：「沈小满呢？」「睡觉。」「那块破木头呢？」他爹老老实实地道：「在我儿子脖子上。睡着呢。」「你家柴垛上，有没有鹅毛？」他爹想了一想，老老实实地道：「有。鸡窝里。」

马小宝使个眼色，一个家丁钻进了鸡窝。鸡窝里登时大乱，那家丁爬出来，一脸的鸡爪印，手里攥着一把鸡毛。马小宝盯着柴垛顶上的人看了半天，越看越觉得这老瘸子坐得古怪，底下不知埋伏着什么，把火把往雪地里一戳：「沈小满藏着什么，我迟早翻出来。」带着人走了。

第二天，果然下了雪。早上，他爹揉着眼睛道：「昨儿夜里，我打呼噜了吗？」小满道：「打了。三遍。」他爹想了一想：「……那是打了。」他娘在灶前道：「你爹昨儿唱了一出空城计。」他爹道：「我不会唱戏。我膝盖疼。」别的，他什么也没说。他娘的账上，这一天记的是：

正月初五。无。爹上柴垛。

隔了一夜，小满再爬上柴垛，发现柴垛朝着路的那一面，高出了一截，一根一根码得严严实实，像一堵墙，从路上望过来，什么也看不见。风吹是吹不成这样的。

马小宝空手而回，却不肯罢休。没过三天，村里便传开了：沈家柴垛上，半夜有人憋气，憋得像个吊死鬼。小满不辩。他在井台边上，当着一圈洗衣裳的婆娘，哆哆嗦嗦地道：「那不是人。是个鬼。白衣裳，没有脚，坐在柴垛上，不喘气——鬼哪有喘气的。我娘夜夜给它上三炷香，它才不进屋。」婆娘们脸都白了。这个鬼，马三去年秋天交租那天就听他说过，那时候它吃饼；他娘说编得不好，鬼不吃饼，该吃香火——如今它改吃香火了。这话当天便传进了马家。有人供着的鬼，马家惹不起，从此天一黑，马家的家丁宁肯绕半里地，也不从沈家屋后过。

他娘听说了，什么也没说，当天夜里真在柴垛底下插了三炷香。账上记着：

正月初九。香三炷，六文。鬼。

刘豆芽那边，却再没有动静。直到二月初二，雁回来的那天夜里，柴垛底下又冒出了那颗脑袋。

刘豆芽手里捏着一把灰白的绒毛，递上来，不敢看他：「……赔你的。」他网着了一只北飞的大雁，雁卖给了马家的厨房，毛他留下了。「那块桂花糕，是馊的。」他道，「我拉了三天。」说完就跑了。

那天夜里，他娘念第五篇，就是当初挑出来「有数」的那一篇。这一回，她从头到尾念全了：「初学行炁，鼻中引炁而闭之，阴以心数至一百二十，乃以口微吐之，及引之，皆不欲令己耳闻其炁出入之声，常令入多出少，以鸿毛著鼻口之上，吐炁而鸿毛不动为候也。」她说，这是一个叫葛洪的人写的。她一句一句讲：鼻子吸，闭住，心里数；嘴里吐，吐得极轻极细，吸和吐都轻到连自己的耳朵也听不见；吸得多，吐得少；鸿毛不动，才算。

这一段前头，还有一句：「得胎息者，能不以鼻口嘘吸，如在胞胎之中，则道成矣。」他娘说，练到头，不用鼻子也不用嘴，像娘肚子里的孩子那样，自己就会「息」。小满想起老周家炕头那个小子，肚子一鼓一瘪，一点声音也没有。那孩子出娘胎才两天，离「胞胎」最近。

他又想起刘豆芽。四十四，是憋出来的；一吐，鹅毛飞过了院子。书上要的不是憋得久，是吐得轻。数是憋出来的，毛是骗不了人的。

他把大雁的绒毛粘上竹篾，搁在鼻子底下。那绒毛比鹅毛轻了一半，他还没开始吐，吸气的时候它就晃了。数到五十二，他一口气细细地吐出去——大雁毛从竹篾上飘了起来，悠悠地，落进了柴堆。

二月初一。鹅毛：满，五十二，毛抖。
二月初二。雁毛：五十二，毛飞。

一个冬天攒下来的，一夜又回到了「毛飞」。他娘把这两行记完，没说话，拿笔在「雁毛」两个字底下，划了一道。

便在这个月里，县城的城门口，贴出了一张告示。

The eyes were Liu Douya's. Liu Douya — Beansprout Liu — was Old Liu's eldest, half a year younger than Xiaoman and thin as a bean sprout, who netted sparrows on winter nights and sold them at two cash apiece. On the night of the tenth of the twelfth month he was crouched at the foot of the Shens' woodpile taking in his net when he looked up and saw white breath rising from the top of the woodpile — one puff, a long, long pause, another puff. In the deep of winter a person's breath shows white; but this breath paused too long, too long to be a living person. The first night he saw the boy finish holding his breath, take a piece of wood from round his neck, hold it in his palm and mutter to it, as if reporting accounts; the second night the same. The third night he crept closer: on top of the woodpile sat a boy with a feather under his nose.

"Shen Xiaoman, what are you doing with a goose feather?" Xiaoman nearly pitched off the woodpile. Liu Douya had already climbed up, eyes darting. "You're here every night. I've watched three nights. Holding your breath, then talking to a piece of wood — casting spells? Tell me, or tomorrow I tell Ma Xiaobao."

Xiaoman's mind spun three times over. The truth meant death; saying *nothing* meant he'd go and tell tomorrow anyway. He said, "Breath-holding contest. Whoever holds longest wins. I'm up against the feather — it doesn't move, I don't breathe." Liu Douya's eyes lit up. "Me too!"

He grabbed the feather, put it under his nose, puffed out his cheeks, sucked in like a bellows and nodded his head once per count, pecking like a hen at grain, twice as fast as Xiaoman; his face went from red to purple, purple to black, and at the forty-fourth nod the breath exploded out of him — *bang*. The feather shot off like a sparrow hit by a musket, straight across the yard into the pigsty. Liu Douya clung to the woodpile panting a long while, and when he'd got his breath back he yelled: "Forty-four! You?" Xiaoman said, "…Thirty-seven."

Liu Douya rolled about on the woodpile laughing. "You practise every night and you can't beat my first go! Tomorrow I'll tell the whole village!" Xiaoman said, "Go on then." He meant it: the whole village knowing Shen Xiaoman lost a breath-holding contest to Liu Douya was a hundred times better than them knowing he was practising something of the immortals.

Still, climbing into the pigsty to fetch the feather, his heart went half cold. He'd counted every night for nearly three months and couldn't out-count Liu Douya on his first try.

In the twelfth month he took Granny Wu a load of firewood — the half he'd hidden at the bottom of the woodpile; hide any more and the pile would collapse.

Granny Wu sat on her threshold listening to him stack it log by log, and when he'd done she said, "One load. Carried by one person. Carried without panting." Only then did Xiaoman remember to pant, and hurriedly panted twice. Granny Wu's three teeth showed. "Panting now's too late." She said again that her three teeth were still there, still hadn't got what they were waiting for. Xiaoman asked what for; she said, "When it comes, they'll know." She reached out and felt his hands, and put them to her nose. "Back-yard earth?" Xiaoman said, "Dad dug it over. Says the soil's gone sour. Smells of rust." Granny Wu faced west for a long while before she said, "In those days, this earth smelled sweet."

Coming back from Granny Wu's, past the threshing floor, he saw the children playing Nine-Headed Snake. A bigger child was the head; the rest held one another's back hems in a chain, each with a hand raised above their head; the head hissed and the ones behind copied him one after another, nine mouths hissing together, so the snake-catcher couldn't tell which was the real head. A good catcher didn't look, he listened: the first hiss is warm; the rest are echoes. The head was Liu Douya. As the chain ran they sang the old song nobody knew who'd made:

"One head eats one mountain,
Two heads eat two rivers,
Three heads eat three granaries,
Four heads eat four fields,
Five heads eat the five grains' seed,
Six heads eat six pens of beasts,
Seven heads eat seven family stoves,
Eight heads eat eight directions' smoke,
Nine heads eat the Nine Provinces —
Ate the Nine Provinces, still cries hungry!"

At "seven heads eat seven family stoves" the singing stopped. Ma Xiaobao came over in his fiery fox-fur jacket, chewing an osmanthus cake. "Nine-Headed Snake? I'll play. I'm the head." Liu Douya slowly lowered his arm and stepped aside. Ma Xiaobao took his place, spread his arms and hissed. Not one child behind him copied. The chain had, at some point, already scattered, each one slipping back to their own doorway to peer out from behind their mother. Ma Xiaobao stood alone on the threshing floor with his arms out for a while, swore "Boring," and kicked a lump of frozen snow flying. Behind some door a child sang softly: "…Ate the Nine Provinces, still cries hungry."

Under the old locust A He was tapping her forehead with a finger: "One head, a mountain; two heads, two rivers…" Xiaoman asked what she was counting that for. She said, "Nine heads ate this much. Somebody has to keep the account."

Xiaoman was about to laugh when the smile froze on his face. At the far side of the threshing floor Liu Douya hadn't left. Ma Xiaobao took an osmanthus cake from his sleeve and handed it over. Liu Douya took a bite, leaned to Ma Xiaobao's ear, said something, and as he spoke measured out a palm's size with his hand and pointed toward the Shens' woodpile.

At New Year the Shens had no meat. His mother made two trays of cabbage dumplings, pushing a little extra filling into each so they all had round bellies, as if they'd eaten their fill. At dusk A He came over with a bowl brimming with braised offal, soy-dark and glossy, and set it on the stove. "My mum braised it. It's not a gift. That set of offal last autumn was worth more than a cabbage, and the difference is what our family owes yours. This bowl pays back the principal. Interest, next year." At the door she turned back to Xiaoman. "You still owe me three and a half. No debt-collecting at New Year."

Keeping the New Year's Eve watch, his mother lit the lamp and read the fourth section: "*Serene and empty, the true breath follows; spirit kept within, whence would illness come?*" His mother said: if the mind doesn't grasp and doesn't hurry, if it's empty, then that *true breath* will be willing to follow you.

Xiaoman took in only half of it. He was carrying a number: the night before, he'd counted to forty-six. If he could pass fifty tonight, the new year would start with a lucky sign. He climbed the woodpile — on New Year's Eve his mother let him — called "Go!", drew a breath, held it, and counted furiously in his head: thirty, forty, forty-five… Inside the window his mother flicked the abacus, one bead, one count. The breath burst out of him and he shouted, "Fifty!" From the window his mother said, "Thirty-eight."

Xiaoman froze on the woodpile. His mother pushed the abacus onto the windowsill. "I flicked it bead by bead at the pace your grandfather taught me. You counted fifty; I flicked thirty-eight." She paused. "That's counting on Liu Douya's behalf. Of all ways to count, only slow can't be beaten."

Xiaoman's face burned. His mother said, "Do you know why you're called Xiaoman?" "…Because I was born on Xiaoman day." "Your father wanted to call you Mancang — full granary, a full granary and a full bin, eat your fill all your life. I said no. When it's full, it spills over. Fill the granary and the rats come; fill the bowl and it slops; fill a person and he doesn't know when he's eaten enough. *Xiaoman* — a little full — is just right: fed a little, not yet full, still knows hunger." She put a peeled chestnut in his mouth. "Counting's the same. The moment you're greedy it's full, and full, it spills."

New Year's Eve. Reported fifty. Actual thirty-eight.

Past midnight Xiaoman was thirteen. He took out the token and said softly, "Happy New Year. I'm thirteen." The token went bright, dim — still asleep. He tucked it back against his chest and, no longer greedy for the number, breathed in and out, counting bead by bead; at forty-one the feather turned over and didn't fly.

Somebody in the village let off a firecracker, a distant *bang*. Xiaoman didn't look; he was looking toward the threshing floor. There was nothing on it, but he remembered Liu Douya's pointing finger. Ma Xiaobao knew. And once Ma Xiaobao knew, he wouldn't stop at knowing half.

Early on the fourth of the first month his father crouched in the snow behind the house and looked a long while. In the snow was a trail of small straw-sandal prints that came round the yard wall and stopped at the foot of the woodpile — more than once; and last night seven or eight pairs of boots had followed the straw sandals round the wall, stood behind the house and trampled a patch flat. His father stood, brushed the snow off his knee, and said only: "Scouting." He went back in, lay down, and snored to the third round.

On the night of the fifth of the first month, Xiaoman didn't go up the woodpile.

He lay on the kang with his eyes open; he'd spent the whole day reckoning: a boy like Ma Xiaobao, hearing "holding his breath on the woodpile", wouldn't think *breath-holding*, he'd think *Shen Xiaoman's hiding something*; and once he thought that, he'd come to search. A feather they could find, no matter; but the bamboo scroll, the token on his chest — he stuffed the scroll into the flue of the kang, held the token in his fist, and listened. In the inner room his father's snoring went on, round after round.

Around midnight, torches flared outside the yard wall. Seven or eight, bobbing — the Mas' men, led by that fiery fox-fur jacket. They didn't come in by the gate; they went round the wall to the back of the house, straight for the woodpile. Xiaoman lay with his eye to a crack in the window, his heart in his throat: at some point his father's snoring had stopped.

The torches surrounded the woodpile. On top of it sat a man wrapped in the ragged cotton quilt, one leg stuck straight out, the knee bound in hemp, sitting square and upright. It was his father.

Ma Xiaobao held up his torch and gaped a long while. "…Old Cripple? What are you doing up there?" His father said, "Knee hurts, can't sleep. Came out to ask the sky." "Ask it what?" "It'll snow tomorrow." Ma Xiaobao shone the torch round. "Where's Shen Xiaoman?" "Asleep." "And that junk wood?" His father said, quite honestly, "Round my son's neck. Asleep." "Any goose feathers on your woodpile?" His father thought about it and said, quite honestly, "Yes. In the henhouse."

Ma Xiaobao jerked his chin, and one of the men crawled into the henhouse. The henhouse erupted; the man crawled out with his face covered in claw marks and a fistful of chicken feathers. Ma Xiaobao stared at the man on the woodpile a long while — the more he looked, the stranger the old cripple sitting there seemed, as if who knew what ambush lay underneath — then stabbed his torch into the snow. "Whatever Shen Xiaoman's hiding, I'll dig it out sooner or later," and led his men away.

The next day, sure enough, it snowed. In the morning his father rubbed his eyes and said, "Last night, did I snore?" Xiaoman said, "You did. Three rounds." His father thought. "…Then I snored." His mother said from the stove, "Your father sang *The Empty City Ruse* last night." His father said, "I can't sing opera. My knee hurts." Apart from that he said nothing at all. In his mother's accounts that day read:

First month, fifth. None. Dad went up the woodpile.

The night after, when Xiaoman climbed the woodpile again, he found the side facing the road had grown a layer taller, the logs stacked tight and close like a wall; from the road you could see nothing. The wind couldn't have blown it like that.

Ma Xiaobao had gone home empty-handed, but he wouldn't let it go. Within three days it was all over the village: on the Shens' woodpile, at midnight, someone held his breath like a hanged ghost. Xiaoman didn't deny it. At the well, in front of a ring of women washing clothes, he said, trembling: "That's not a person. It's a ghost. White clothes, no feet, sits on the woodpile, doesn't breathe — what ghost breathes? My mum burns three sticks of incense for it every night, so it won't come into the house." The women went white. The story reached the Ma house that same day. This ghost Ma San had heard of before, on rent day last autumn — back then it ate flatbread; his mother had said it was a bad story, ghosts don't eat flatbread, they should eat incense — and now it had switched to incense. A ghost with someone feeding it the Mas didn't dare cross; from then on, after dark, the Mas' men would sooner go half a li round than pass behind the Shens' house.

His mother heard, said nothing, and that very night really did stick three sticks of incense at the foot of the woodpile. The accounts read:

First month, ninth. Incense, three sticks, six cash. Ghost.

From Liu Douya's side, though, nothing more. Until the second of the second month, the night the wild geese came back, when that head popped up at the foot of the woodpile again.

Liu Douya held up a handful of grey-white down without looking at him. "…To make up to you." He'd netted a wild goose flying north, sold the goose to the Ma kitchen, and kept the feathers. "That osmanthus cake had gone off," he said. "I had the runs three days." With that he ran.

That night his mother read the fifth section — the one she'd first picked out for having *a number in it*. This time she read it whole: "*When first learning to move the breath, draw it in through the nose and hold it; count silently in the heart to a hundred and twenty, then let it out very softly through the mouth. Both drawing in and letting out, let not your own ears hear the sound of the breath going in and out; always let more go in than comes out. Lay a wild-goose feather over nose and mouth: when you breathe out and the feather does not stir, that is the sign.*" She said a man called Ge Hong wrote it. She explained it line by line: in through the nose, hold, count in your head; out through the mouth, out very light and fine; drawing in and letting out both so light even your own ears can't hear; take in more, let out less; only when the feather doesn't move does it count.

Before that passage there was one more line: "*One who has attained womb-breathing can breathe without nose or mouth, as in the womb; then the Way is complete.*" His mother said: practise it to the end and you need neither nose nor mouth; like a baby in its mother's belly you just *breathe* of yourself. Xiaoman thought of the little boy at the head of Old Zhou's kang, belly rising and falling without a sound. That baby had been two days out of the womb — the nearest to *the womb* of anyone.

He thought of Liu Douya, too. Forty-four, forced out by holding; one breath out, and the feather flew across the yard. What the book wanted wasn't holding long; it was breathing out light. The number can be forced; the feather can't be fooled.

He stuck the wild-goose down on the bamboo strip and put it under his nose. The down was half the weight of the goose feather; it swayed while he was still breathing in. At fifty-two he let the breath out, fine and thin — and the wild-goose down floated up off the bamboo, drifting, and settled in the woodpile.

Second month, first. Goose feather: Man, fifty-two, feather trembled.
Second month, second. Wild-goose down: fifty-two, feather flew.

A whole winter's saving, and in one night he was back to *feather flew*. His mother finished those two lines, said nothing, and drew a line under the words *wild-goose down*.

That same month, at the gate of the county town, a notice was posted.
